                                                Adam Snapp
                                              Rebuttal Testimony

    1    Q.    Please state your name and business address.
    2    A.    My name is Adam Snapp. My business address is 321 North Harvey, Oklahoma City,
    3          Oklahoma 73102.
    4
    5    Q.    By whom are you employed and in what capacity?
    6    A.    I am employed by Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or “Company”) as
    7          Director of Transmission Planning.
    8
    9    Q.    Please summarize your professional qualifications and educational background.
   10    A.    I earned a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Oklahoma Christian
   11          University in 2011, and a Master of Science in Engineering from Oklahoma Christian in
   12          2012. I also earned a Master of Business Administration with focus on Finance from
   13          Oklahoma Christian in 2015. I have been a Professional Engineer in Oklahoma since 2015.
   14          I have been with OG&E since 2011. During my time at OG&E, I have worked with several
   15          different teams, including system protection, distribution engineering, asset management,
   16          substation operations, SCADA EMS, transmission planning, and transmission and
   17          substation design. My current title is Director of Transmission Planning and I have been
   18          in my current position since 2022.
   19
   20    Q.    What is the purpose of your testimony in this proceeding?
   21    A.    I respond to three issues raised by Google witness Adrian Kimbrough.           First, Mr.
   22          Kimbrough recommends reducing the XLPL power factor requirement from 98% to 90%.1
   23          Second, Mr. Kimbrough recommends that OG&E be required to evaluate alternatives to
   24          transmission upgrades, including Grid Enhancing Technologies (“GETs”). 2 Third, I
   25          address his recommendation that XLPL customers be permitted to self-build dedicated




         1
               Responsive Testimony of Adrian Kimbrough, 32:20–35:13.

    1          interconnection facilities,3 supplementing the Rebuttal Testimony of OG&E witness John
    2          Laws from a transmission planning perspective.
    3
    4                                          POWER FACTOR
    5    Q.    What is power factor?
    6    A.    Power factor measures how effectively electrical power is converted into useful work. It
    7          is the ratio of real power, measured in megawatts, to apparent power, which includes both
    8          real power and the reactive power needed to maintain electric and magnetic fields in certain
    9          equipment. A power factor closer to 100% means that more of the electrical capacity
   10          supplied is being used to perform useful work.
   11
   12    Q.    Why is power factor important to the reliable and efficient operation of the electric
   13          system?
   14    A.    A lower power factor requires the electric system to supply more reactive power and carry
   15          more current to deliver the same amount of useful power. Reactive power is measured in
   16          megavolt-amperes reactive, or MVAR. Although MVAR does not perform useful work, it
   17          is necessary to maintain system voltage and support the electric and magnetic fields used
   18          by certain equipment. Because reactive power does not travel efficiently over long
   19          distances, it generally must be supplied near the location where it is consumed. Large
   20          MVAR requirements consume transmission and generation capability, increase electrical
   21          losses and equipment heating, and leave less operating margin to respond to the loss of a
   22          line, transformer, or generator. If sufficient reactive support is unavailable, voltage can
   23          decline and, in severe conditions, lead to protective load shedding and/or broader voltage
   24          instability. Maintaining a higher power factor therefore reduces the MVAR requirement at
   25          its source, preserves system capacity and contingency margin, and helps OG&E maintain
   26          reliable and efficient service to customers.




         3
               Id. at 26:20-22.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                     Page 3 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 14




    1    Q.    Google witness Adrian Kimbrough recommends reducing the XLPL power factor
    2          requirement from 98% to 90%.4 Do you agree?
    3    A.    No. I do not agree. A 90% power factor standard may be reasonable for traditional
    4          customer classes, but it is not appropriate for customers taking service under the XLPL
    5          tariff. The customers eligible for XLPL service are orders of magnitude larger than the
    6          customers typically served under other tariff schedules. As a result, even relatively small
    7          reductions in power factor can create very large reactive power requirements that impose
    8          significant costs and operational challenges on the transmission system. The potential
    9          impacts associated with 200 MW, 500 MW, or 1,000 MW customers are fundamentally
   10          different than the impacts associated with a traditional commercial customer and therefore
   11          warrant a more stringent requirement.
   12
   13    Q.    Please explain why reactive power requirements become more significant for XLPL
   14          customers.
   15    A.    Reactive power requirements increase substantially as customer load grows. For example,
   16          a 20 MW load operating at a 90% power factor requires approximately 9.7 MVAR of
   17          reactive support. By comparison, a 200 MW load operating at a 98% power factor requires
   18          approximately 41 MVAR of reactive support. While 41 MVAR is significant, it is generally
   19          within the range of transmission-level capacitor equipment routinely installed on utility
   20          systems.
   21                  However, if a 200 MW XLPL customer were permitted to operate at a 90% power
   22          factor, the reactive power requirement would increase to approximately 97 MVAR. That
   23          amount would exceed the size of every transmission capacitor installed on OG&E’s system
   24          today. The challenge becomes even more severe for larger XLPL customers. A 1,000 MW
   25          customer operating at a 90% power factor would require approximately 500 MVAR of
   26          reactive support, an amount that would greatly exceed the capability of any single reactive
   27          device currently installed on OG&E’s system and likely unable to be implemented at all.
   28          At 98% power factor, the requirements are 200 MVAR for that same 1,000 MW load which
   29          is a more reasonable amount and is much more technically feasible.



         4
               Id. at 32:20–35:13.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                    Page 4 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 14




    1    Q.    Google witness Adrian Kimbrough suggests that the 98% requirement is
    2          “exceptionally stringent”.5 How do you respond?
    3    A.    The recommendation does not adequately recognize the unique reliability challenges
    4          associated with serving customers of this size.         Very large reactive devices create
    5          operational challenges that do not exist at smaller load levels. As capacitor installations
    6          become larger, switching operations can produce voltage fluctuations and flicker. Reactive
    7          devices large enough to support XLPL customers operating at a 90% power factor could
    8          create switching events severe enough to affect nearby customers or the XLPL customer
    9          itself. These effects could include loss of service for the XLPL customer and other
   10          customers within close electrical proximity. Consequently, maintaining a more stringent
   11          power factor requirement at the customer level reduces the need for very large utility-
   12          owned reactive support equipment and improves operational reliability.
   13
   14    Q.    Why is this important from a cost causation perspective?
   15    A.    If XLPL customers are allowed to operate at lower power factors, OG&E would be required
   16          to construct, operate, and maintain substantial additional reactive support facilities in order
   17          to serve those customers and maintain acceptable system voltages. Those costs would
   18          ultimately be borne through the transmission system and would create the potential for cost
   19          shifts to other customers. Requiring XLPL customers to maintain a high power factor is
   20          consistent with cost-causation principles because it places responsibility for reactive power
   21          management on the customer creating the need for that support instead of OG&E’s existing
   22          customers.
   23
   24    Q.    Are there additional reliability concerns associated with lower power factors?
   25    A.    Yes. Maintaining system voltage within acceptable operating limits is one of the most
   26          important responsibilities of a transmission operator. Large reactive power demands make
   27          voltage control significantly more difficult. OG&E’s transmission protection systems may
   28          be designed to automatically shed load or isolate portions of the system if voltages move
   29          outside predetermined operating limits. These protections exist to prevent cascading



         5
               Id. at 32:20–33:1.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                       Page 5 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 14




    1          outages and widespread system disturbances. Requiring XLPL customers to maintain a
    2          98% power factor helps reduce the likelihood that a single large load could adversely affect
    3          system voltage performance and reliability for other customers.
    4
    5    Q.    Does a poor power factor affect generation resources as well?
    6    A.    Yes.   Reactive power requirements affect not only transmission facilities but also
    7          generation resources. When generation resources must produce additional reactive power
    8          to support large loads, those resources operate less efficiently and experience increased
    9          electrical losses. As a result, more generation resources may be necessary to serve the same
   10          amount of real customer load. If XLPL customers are permitted to operate at substantially
   11          lower power factors, the resulting increase in generation and transmission requirements
   12          could impose costs on other customers that receive no corresponding benefit.
   13
   14    Q.    What is your recommendation regarding the proposed 98% power factor
   15          requirement?
   16    A.    I recommend that the Commission approve the 98% power factor requirement as proposed.
   17          XLPL customers are uniquely positioned to create very large reactive power requirements
   18          that can impact transmission reliability, voltage stability, generation efficiency, and
   19          customer costs. Holding XLPL customers to a more rigorous power factor standard than
   20          traditional rate classes is appropriate and necessary to ensure that the costs and operational
   21          impacts associated with serving those loads are not shifted to other customers. The
   22          proposed 98% standard is a reasonable customer protection measure that supports both
   23          reliability and cost causation principles.




         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                      Page 6 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 14




    1                             GRID ENHANCING TECHNOLOGIES
    2    Q.    Google witness Adrian Kimbrough recommends requiring OG&E to evaluate Grid
    3          Enhancing Technologies (“GETs”), advanced conductors, and other alternatives
    4          before implementing transmission upgrades for XLPL customers.6 Do you agree?
    5    A.    No. OG&E already evaluates GETs and other transmission technologies where appropriate
    6          as part of its routine transmission planning process and has done so for many years. The
    7          Company’s responsibility is to identify the most cost-effective and reliable long-term
    8          solution for the transmission system as a whole. The suggestion that transmission planning
    9          studies should be required to identify or favor any specific technology before determining
   10          the nature of a transmission constraint is not consistent with sound transmission planning
   11          practices.
   12
   13    Q.    Why should transmission planning remain technology neutral?
   14    A.    Transmission planning studies are intended to identify system constraints and determine
   15          what infrastructure is required to reliably serve load under a broad range of operating
   16          conditions. Those studies should be technology neutral. In other words, the planning
   17          process should first determine what system needs exist and then evaluate the most
   18          appropriate solution to address that need. Predetermining that a particular technology such
   19          as dynamic line ratings, topology optimization, or advanced conductors must be considered
   20          or preferred before identifying the constraint risks biasing the planning process toward a
   21          particular outcome rather than the most appropriate engineering solution.
   22                  OG&E’s transmission planners and engineers already evaluate available
   23          technologies and alternatives when determining how best to address identified system
   24          needs. The Company’s objective is to provide reliable service at the lowest reasonable cost
   25          to all customers, and therefore OG&E is inherently incentivized to identify the most cost-
   26          effective solution when addressing transmission constraints.




         6
               Id. at 28:10–16.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                    Page 7 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 14




    1    Q.    Google witness Kimbrough recommends that OG&E evaluate dynamic line ratings
    2          before undertaking more traditional transmission upgrades.7 Are dynamic line
    3          ratings an appropriate substitute for transmission upgrades?
    4    A.    Generally no. Dynamic line ratings serve a fundamentally different purpose than long-
    5          term transmission upgrades. Dynamic line ratings temporarily increase transmission line
    6          ratings when favorable environmental conditions are present, such as lower temperatures
    7          or higher wind speeds. However, they may also reduce transmission line ratings when
    8          those environmental conditions cease to exist. Relying on dynamic line ratings in the peak
    9          of summer when winds are historically low, would be especially problematic.
   10                  Because load-serving obligations must be planned around conditions that are
   11          reasonably expected to occur during peak system usage, dynamic line ratings are not an
   12          appropriate substitute for long-term transmission infrastructure needed to reliably serve
   13          load. OG&E plans its transmission system using assumptions that reflect historical weather
   14          conditions and expected peak operating conditions within its service territory. Static
   15          ratings provide a predictable indication of when transmission constraints will occur and
   16          allow appropriate upgrades to be identified and implemented before reliability concerns
   17          develop.
   18
   19    Q.    What about topology optimization?
   20    A.    Topology optimization is likewise not a substitute for permanent transmission
   21          infrastructure.      Topology optimization generally involves temporary switching
   22          configurations intended to improve the efficiency of wholesale market operations. While
   23          those actions may improve economic dispatch under certain operating conditions, they
   24          often have limited impact on the amount of load that can reliably be served under long-
   25          term planning conditions.
   26                  Because topology optimization relies on temporary operating configurations, it
   27          cannot be relied upon during transmission planning and load interconnection studies that
   28          are intended to identify the permanent network upgrades necessary to reliably connect large
   29          loads to the grid.



         7
               Id. at 27:12–17.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                    Page 8 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 14




    1    Q.    Google witness Kimbrough also recommends requiring OG&E to evaluate advanced
    2          conductors before implementing conventional rebuilds.8 Do you agree?
    3    A.    No. Advanced conductors may be an appropriate solution in some circumstances, but they
    4          are not universally applicable and should not be presumed to be superior to traditional
    5          transmission upgrades.
    6                  Many transmission facilities currently in service were constructed decades ago and
    7          have been operating well beyond their original anticipated lives. The structures supporting
    8          those lines were often not designed to withstand the mechanical tensions associated with
    9          many advanced conductor technologies. In addition, some advanced conductors increase
   10          capacity by their ability to operate at substantially higher temperatures than traditional
   11          ACSR conductors, which can increase conductor sag and create clearance and safety
   12          concerns if not carefully evaluated.
   13                  As a result, it is not always possible or economic to simply replace an existing
   14          conductor with an advanced conductor while utilizing the existing line structures.
   15
   16    Q.    Do advanced conductors always improve system efficiency?
   17    A.    No. It is important to distinguish between increased capacity and increased efficiency.
   18          Many advanced conductors achieve additional capacity by operating at substantially higher
   19          temperatures than traditional conductors. While those higher operating temperatures can
   20          increase line capacity, higher temperatures also result in increased electrical losses.
   21                  Those losses must ultimately be supplied by additional generation resources.
   22          Consequently, a solution that maximizes transmission capacity relying solely on the
   23          installation of an advanced conductor is not necessarily the solution that minimizes
   24          lifecycle system costs. In some circumstances, a traditional line rebuild may provide a
   25          more economical outcome when total lifecycle costs, losses, reliability, maintenance
   26          requirements, efficiency, and safety considerations are evaluated together.




         8
               Id. at 28:10–16.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                       Page 9 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 14




    1    Q.    Google witness Kimbrough recommends requiring OG&E to provide detailed
    2          engineering studies and obtain customer review before proceeding with certain
    3          transmission solutions.9 Would such a requirement be beneficial?
    4    A.    No. Such a requirement would increase costs and delay implementation without providing
    5          corresponding benefits. OG&E already performs the engineering analyses necessary to
    6          identify reliable and cost-effective solutions. Imposing additional mandatory studies
    7          focused on specific technologies would increase the cost and administrative burden of
    8          serving new loads without demonstrating that the resulting decisions would be better.
    9                  Moreover, requiring review, feedback, or approval from a particular XLPL
   10          customer before implementation of transmission solutions could adversely affect OG&E’s
   11          ability to provide timely service. If transmission upgrades provide benefits beyond a single
   12          customer, delaying those upgrades while additional studies and customer review processes
   13          occur would delay the broader reliability and economic benefits that the upgrades provide
   14          to all customers.
   15
   16    Q.    What is your recommendation regarding Google’s proposed transmission planning
   17          modifications?
   18    A.    I recommend the Commission reject proposals that would require OG&E to conduct
   19          technology-specific analyses or otherwise prejudice transmission planning studies toward
   20          particular technologies. OG&E should continue to be permitted to identify transmission
   21          needs through technology-neutral reliability studies and then evaluate available solutions,
   22          including GETs, advanced conductors, conventional rebuilds, and other alternatives, to
   23          determine the most cost-effective and appropriate long-term solution.
   24                  Mandating the consideration of specific technologies or requiring customer
   25          approval processes would increase costs, delay implementation timelines, and potentially
   26          undermine reliability objectives without providing meaningful additional protection to
   27          customers. The better approach is to allow OG&E’s transmission planners to evaluate all
   28          available solutions and implement the option that best balances long-term reliability,
   29          affordability, safety, and operational performance for all customers.



         9
               Ibid.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                   Page 10 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046

    1              CUSTOMER SELF-BUILD OF INTERCONNECTION FACILITIES
    2    Q.    Google witness Adrian Kimbrough recommends that XLPL customers be permitted
    3          to self-build dedicated interconnection facilities.           Do you agree with that
    4          recommendation?
    5    A.     No. As OG&E witness John Laws explains in his Rebuttal Testimony, facilities
    6          interconnecting an XLPL customer to OG&E’s transmission system become part of the
    7          system OG&E must operate, maintain, and answer for, regardless of who constructed them.
    8          I agree with Mr. Laws and offer several additional observations from a transmission
    9          planning perspective.
   10                 Transmission interconnection facilities cannot be planned or constructed as stand-
   11          alone customer assets. By definition, they are a part of the Bulk Electric System (BES)
   12          and their construction impacts not only the customer who is connecting at that location but
   13          the reliability of every customer connected to the BES.
   14                 This concept of self-build comes up often in Generation Interconnection studies.
   15          The SPP/FERC pro-forma GIA considers the concept of self-building interconnection
   16          facilities. When those facilities are expansions of existing facilities (such as we’re
   17          discussing here for customer interconnect facilities), FERC has determined that it is not
   18          appropriate for the interconnection customer to build such facilities but rather the standard
   19          option of the Transmission Owner building and constructing these facilities is the de facto
   20          outcome.
   21                 These facilities will be owned and operated by OG&E. It will be OG&E’s
   22          responsibility to maintain them for their entire lifecycle, and it is important that the
   23          facilities are built to OG&E standards, using OG&E manufacturer specifications. Field
   24          personnel who maintain and operate this equipment are trained in how to safely operate
   25          OG&E designed and constructed facilities. Allowing a customer to build assets that OG&E
   26          members will maintain creates safety risks that are not present otherwise.
   27                 Additionally, OG&E’s maintenance and restoration plans, as well as our spare parts
   28          inventory strategies are built around a set of standard designs. If XLPL customers were to
   29          build facilities that did not match OG&E standards, any potential outages that might occur
   30          when their equipment fails would become prolonged outages, causing unnecessarily
   31          detrimental operational impact.

         Rebuttal Testimony of Adam Snapp                                                    Page 11 of 13
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 65 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 14




    1                 In sum, allowing XLPL customers to construct dedicated interconnection facilities
    2          introduces unnecessary safety risks for O&GE members and contractors, operational
    3          challenges, prolongs restoration in the event of equipment failure, introduces additional
    4          engineering complexity, and presents reliability risks for all customers who are connected
    5          to the BES.
    6
    7    Q.    Does your testimony address all issues raised by parties in their responsive testimony?
    8    A.    No. My Rebuttal Testimony is limited in scope and does not address all issues raised in
    9          this proceeding. My silence on any issue should not be construed as agreement with
   10          another party’s testimony.
   11
   12    Q.    Does this conclude your Rebuttal Testimony?
   13    A.    Yes.
